meta.title: Who really said "Patience, and shuffle the cards"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Cervantes wrote it in Don Quixote, Part II — but the speaker is an enchanted knight in a dream, and "the cards" is the translator’s.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Patience, and shuffle the cards'?
meta.ogDescription: Don Quixote, Part II, ch. 23. The speaker is the enchanted Durandarte; the Spanish is just "paciencia y barajar".

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Cervantes wrote it in Don Quixote, Part II (1615), chapter 23. In Spanish it is three words — “paciencia y barajar” — and it is not Don Quixote or Sancho who says it, but Durandarte, an enchanted knight lying on a marble tomb inside the Cave of Montesinos, in a vision Cervantes goes out of his way to call apocryphal. The familiar English wording is Tobias Smollett’s (1755) and Pierre Antoine Motteux’s (1701).

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Durandarte, an enchanted knight — a character within Don Quixote’s vision

source.excerpt: “And if that should not be the case,” replied the afflicted Durandarte, in a faint and languid tone; “and if that should not be the case, cousin, I say, patience, and shuffle the cards.” Then turning himself upon one side, he relapsed into his usual silence, without speaking another word.
trail: Downloaded the full text of Smollett’s 1755 translation ↗ from Project Gutenberg and searched it. “Patience, and shuffle the cards” appears twice: in Durandarte’s speech, and again when the scholar cousin quotes it back.

Did the same with Motteux’s translation ↗, which gives the identical English at the identical point, and with Ormsby’s 1885 translation ↗, which renders it “patience and shuffle” and labels the chapter as Part II, chapter XXIII.
Confirmed the Spanish in Gutenberg’s Spanish Don Quijote ↗: “cuando así no sea, ¡oh primo!, digo, paciencia y barajar” — the same sentence, in the same place.
Wikiquote’s Cervantes page ↗ lists “I say patience, and shuffle the cards” under Part II (1615), Ch. 23, agreeing with all four texts.
source.excerptNote: Translators split on the last three words. Smollett (1755) and Motteux (1701) both give “patience, and shuffle the cards”; John Ormsby (1885) keeps it tight as “patience and shuffle”. The Spanish barajar means to shuffle — the cards are supplied by the English.
source.rightsNote: Free to use. The Spanish original was published in 1615, and every English translation quoted here is long out of copyright in the United States: Motteux 1701, Smollett 1755, Ormsby 1885 — all well before the 1931 cut-off, and all available in full at Project Gutenberg.

author.name: Miguel de Cervantes
author.heading: About Miguel de Cervantes
author.bio: Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra lost the use of his left hand at Lepanto, spent five years as a captive in Algiers, and worked as a tax collector before publishing the first part of Don Quixote in 1605 at fifty-seven. The second part followed in 1615, a year before his death. It is routinely called the first modern novel, and it is stuffed with proverbs — many of which, like this one, escaped the book and became sayings in their own right.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The Cave of Montesinos is the strangest episode in the book. Don Quixote is lowered into a pit on a rope, hauled out a little better than an hour later, by Sancho’s reckoning, and reports having spent three days underground among enchanted knights. Cervantes titles the chapter to say the adventure should be “deemed apocryphal” — he is telling you not to believe his own hero.

Durandarte, whose heart was famously carried to the lady Belerma after his death at Roncesvalles, is lying on his tomb waiting for the enchantment to lift. Told that Don Quixote may be the one to break it, he answers, in effect: and if not, deal again.
detailsBody: Cervantes then makes a joke of the line. A scholar travelling with Don Quixote seizes on it as evidence for the book he is writing, a supplement to Polydore Vergil on the invention of antiquities: since Durandarte died in the time of Charlemagne and could not have learned the phrase while enchanted, playing cards must be that old.

It is a small piece of comic pedantry — a man deducing the history of card games from a ghost’s figure of speech — and it is why the line gets said twice: once by Durandarte in chapter 23, and again by the cousin in the chapter that follows. Being said twice is part of why it stuck.

What survives in circulation is the proverb stripped of all of it: no cave, no enchanted knight, no joke. Just three words of Spanish patience, wearing an English deck of cards the original never mentions.

sourcesVerified.claim: Smollett’s 1755 translation contains "patience, and shuffle the cards" in Durandarte’s speech in the Cave of Montesinos, and again when the scholar cousin repeats it.
Motteux’s translation gives "patience, and shuffle the cards" at the same point in the same chapter.
Ormsby’s 1885 translation renders the line "patience and shuffle" and places it in Part II, chapter XXIII, the Cave of Montesinos chapter.
The Spanish text reads "cuando así no sea, ¡oh primo!, digo, paciencia y barajar" in Durandarte’s speech.
Wikiquote lists "I say patience, and shuffle the cards" under Don Quixote Part II (1615), Ch. 23.
The Cueva de Montesinos is a real cave in La Mancha associated with the episode.
